power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. text.text: Callous-unemotional (CU) traits reflect low empathy, guilt, and concern for others and are associated with persistent antisocial behavior, aggression, and delinquency.
Although CU traits vary across adolescence, less is known about factors predicting increases versus decreases in severity.

Using four annual assessments spanning early to middle adolescence from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development Social Development (ABCD-SD) Study, we characterized CU trajectories using latent class growth analysis and examined changes in CU severity between annual assessments.
Logistic regression tested whether parenting and emotion dysregulation prospectively distinguished shifts in CU severity among adolescents who moved between categories.
Three developmental trajectories emerged: Low (46.9%), Moderate (40.1%), and Elevated (13.0%).

Among adolescents beginning at moderate severity, greater positive parenting was associated with movement to low rather than elevated CU severity (OR = 0.69, p < .001), whereas greater negative parenting (OR = 1.21, p = .024) and emotion dysregulation (OR = 1.18, p = .036) were associated with movement to elevated rather than low severity.
text.formatted: Among adolescents beginning at moderate severity, greater positive parenting was associated with movement to low rather than elevated CU severity (OR = 0.69, p < .001), whereas greater negative parenting (OR = 1.21, p = .024) and emotion dysregulation (OR = 1.18, p = .036) were associated with movement to elevated rather than low severity.

text.text: Among adolescents beginning at low severity, greater positive parenting was associated with movement to moderate rather than directly to elevated severity (OR = 0.82, p = .045), whereas greater emotion dysregulation was associated with movement directly to elevated rather than moderate severity (OR = 1.37, p = .003).

These findings demonstrate that CU trajectories can remain relatively stable at the group level even as adolescents show year-to-year shifts in CU severity, and identify parenting and emotion dysregulation as prospective predictors and potentially modifiable targets for reducing CU traits.
Callous-unemotional (CU) traits are characterized by limited empathy and guilt, reduced concern for others, and shallow or diminished emotional expression (Frick et al., 2014).
text.formatted: Callous-unemotional (CU) traits are characterized by limited empathy and guilt, reduced concern for others, and shallow or diminished emotional expression <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Frick et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Elevated CU traits have also been longitudinally associated with aggression, delinquency, violence, substance use, and adverse social and functional outcomes (Baskin-Sommers et al., 2015; Fontaine et al., 2011; McMahon et al., 2010).
text.formatted: Elevated CU traits have also been longitudinally associated with aggression, delinquency, violence, substance use, and adverse social and functional outcomes <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Baskin-Sommers et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Fontaine et al., 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">McMahon et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: Despite their association with persistent behavioral difficulties, CU traits are not uniformly stable across adolescence; youth differ in both their overall levels of CU traits and how these traits change over time (Fanti et al., 2017; Fontaine et al., 2011; Simmons et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Despite their association with persistent behavioral difficulties, CU traits are not uniformly stable across adolescence; youth differ in both their overall levels of CU traits and how these traits change over time <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Fanti et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Fontaine et al., 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Simmons et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Person-centered longitudinal studies have captured these differences by classifying youth according to their patterns of CU traits across multiple assessments.

Research spanning adolescence and early adulthood has identified relatively stable low, moderate, and high CU trajectories (Baskin-Sommers et al., 2015), whereas studies beginning earlier in development have identified more heterogeneous developmental patterns, including increasing and decreasing patterns of CU traits alone or jointly with conduct problems (Fanti et al., 2017; Fontaine et al., 2011).
text.formatted: Research spanning adolescence and early adulthood has identified relatively stable low, moderate, and high CU trajectories <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Baskin-Sommers et al., 2015)</ref>, whereas studies beginning earlier in development have identified more heterogeneous developmental patterns, including increasing and decreasing patterns of CU traits alone or jointly with conduct problems <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Fanti et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Fontaine et al., 2011)</ref>.

text.text: However, because trajectory approaches summarize each youth's overall pattern across assessments (Baskin-Sommers et al., 2015; Fanti et al., 2017; Simmons et al., 2024), they can obscure shifts between severity levels that some youth experience along the way.
text.formatted: However, because trajectory approaches summarize each youth's overall pattern across assessments <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Baskin-Sommers et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Fanti et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Simmons et al., 2024)</ref>, they can obscure shifts between severity levels that some youth experience along the way.

text.text: Consequently, less is known about the frequency and predictors of shifts in CU severity.
Parenting is one factor that may contribute to adolescents' shifts in CU severity.

A substantial literature has linked dimensions of parenting, including warmth, involvement, harshness, monitoring, and discipline, to CU traits across childhood and adolescence (Waller et al., 2013; Waller & Hyde, 2017).
text.formatted: A substantial literature has linked dimensions of parenting, including warmth, involvement, harshness, monitoring, and discipline, to CU traits across childhood and adolescence <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Waller et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Waller & Hyde, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Longitudinal studies have linked harsh parenting with higher subsequent CU traits, whereas greater parental warmth and positive parenting have been associated with lower subsequent CU traits (Waller et al., 2012 (Waller et al., , 2014)).
text.formatted: Longitudinal studies have linked harsh parenting with higher subsequent CU traits, whereas greater parental warmth and positive parenting have been associated with lower subsequent CU traits <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(Waller et al., 2012</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Waller et al., , 2014))</ref>.

text.text: Lower parental involvement, monitoring, and knowledge have also been associated with more elevated developmental trajectories (Waller, Baskin-Sommers, & Hyde, 2018).
text.formatted: Lower parental involvement, monitoring, and knowledge have also been associated with more elevated developmental trajectories <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Waller, Baskin-Sommers, & Hyde, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Genetically informed research has further examined the extent to which associations between parenting and CU traits reflect environmental versus genetic influences.

Research with monozygotic twins has linked greater parental warmth with lower CU traits and greater harshness with higher CU traits beyond genetically mediated effects (Waller, Hyde, et al., 2018), although more recent genetically informed longitudinal work suggests that effects of negative parenting on CU traits may be small and partially attributable to genetic and shared environmental influences (Pezzoli et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Research with monozygotic twins has linked greater parental warmth with lower CU traits and greater harshness with higher CU traits beyond genetically mediated effects <ref type="bibr">(Waller, Hyde, et al., 2018)</ref>, although more recent genetically informed longitudinal work suggests that effects of negative parenting on CU traits may be small and partially attributable to genetic and shared environmental influences <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Pezzoli et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Parenting has also been associated with developmental change in CU traits: changes in maternal involvement have accompanied increases and decreases in CU traits during childhood (Fanti et al., 2017), and negative parenting has been associated with within-person increases in CU traits during adolescence (Simmons et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Parenting has also been associated with developmental change in CU traits: changes in maternal involvement have accompanied increases and decreases in CU traits during childhood <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Fanti et al., 2017)</ref>, and negative parenting has been associated with within-person increases in CU traits during adolescence <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Simmons et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Together, this literature suggests that parenting is associated not only with adolescents' levels of CU traits, but also with their developmental course.

Although prior research has linked parenting to CU severity and developmental change, less is known about whether parenting distinguishes adolescents whose CU severity increases from those whose severity decreases.
Emotion dysregulation may also contribute to changes in CU traits across adolescence.

Emotion dysregulation is characterized by difficulties in emotional awareness and clarity, impulse control, goal-directed behavior when distressed, acceptance of emotional experiences, and access to effective regulation strategies (Gratz & Roemer, 2004).
text.formatted: Emotion dysregulation is characterized by difficulties in emotional awareness and clarity, impulse control, goal-directed behavior when distressed, acceptance of emotional experiences, and access to effective regulation strategies <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Gratz & Roemer, 2004)</ref>.

text.text: These difficulties have been linked to multiple forms of child and adolescent psychopathology, including aggression, impulsivity, and conduct problems (Paulus et al., 2021).
text.formatted: These difficulties have been linked to multiple forms of child and adolescent psychopathology, including aggression, impulsivity, and conduct problems <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Paulus et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Although CU traits have historically been associated with reduced emotional responsiveness, youth with elevated CU traits vary considerably in their emotional functioning, and emotion dysregulation is evident among at least some youth with elevated CU traits (Craig & Moretti, 2019; Craig et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Although CU traits have historically been associated with reduced emotional responsiveness, youth with elevated CU traits vary considerably in their emotional functioning, and emotion dysregulation is evident among at least some youth with elevated CU traits <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Craig & Moretti, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Craig et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Recent prospective evidence also suggests that emotion regulation difficulties are associated with subsequent CU traits during childhood (Wilke et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Recent prospective evidence also suggests that emotion regulation difficulties are associated with subsequent CU traits during childhood <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Wilke et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: However, longitudinal research examining whether emotion dysregulation predicts developmental change in CU traits remains limited, particularly during adolescence.
Therefore, as with parenting, it remains unclear whether emotion dysregulation distinguishes how adolescents' CU severity changes over time.
The present study addresses these gaps using longitudinal data from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development Social Development (ABCD-SD) Study.
We examine three questions: (1) What developmental trajectories of CU traits emerge across adolescence?
( 2) To what extent do adolescents remain within the same CU severity level over time?

text.text: and (3) Among adolescents who shift between CU severity levels, do parenting and emotion dysregulation predict the direction or magnitude of these shifts?

Based on prior trajectory research, we first hypothesized that low, moderate, and elevated CU trajectories would emerge and would differ primarily in overall CU severity rather than rates of change (Baskin-Sommers et al., 2015).
text.formatted: Based on prior trajectory research, we first hypothesized that low, moderate, and elevated CU trajectories would emerge and would differ primarily in overall CU severity rather than rates of change <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Baskin-Sommers et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Our second question, concerning the extent to which adolescents remained at stable CU severity over time, was exploratory.

Third, based on longitudinal evidence linking dimensions of parenting to subsequent CU traits (Fanti et al., 2017; Simmons et al., 2024; Waller et al., 2013; Waller, Baskin-Sommers, & Hyde, 2018) and prospective evidence linking emotion regulation difficulties to subsequent CU traits (Wilke et al., 2026), we hypothesized that greater positive parenting would predict movement toward relatively lower severity, whereas greater negative parenting and emotion dysregulation would predict movement toward relatively higher severity among adolescents whose CU severity changed. text.text: The present study focused on four annual assessments of callous-unemotional (CU) traits collected during ABCD-SD waves S02-S05.

These waves were selected because they provided repeated assessments of CU traits spanning early to middle adolescence and allowed for both longitudinal trajectory analyses and examination of wave-to-wave transitions in CU severity.
The ABCD Study received centralized institutional review board approval from the University of California, San Diego, and participating study sites received local institutional review board approval.
Informed consent and assent were obtained in accordance with study procedures.
Across S02-S05, CU data were available for 2,297 youth, who contributed data at between one and four waves.
Age data from linked core ABCD assessments were available for 2,288 participants (99.6%).
At the earliest available corresponding core ABCD assessment, participants' mean age was 12.02 years (SD = 0.70).
Among participants with available sex data, 47.9% were female.

Additional demographic characteristics, including race/ethnicity, household income, highest caregiver education, and caregiver partnership/employment status, are presented in Online Resource 1, Table S1.

text.text: Comparisons between adolescents included in and excluded from the LCGA, using the earliest available nonmissing demographic observations from the core ABCD dataset, revealed statistically significant differences in recorded age, household income, highest caregiver education, and caregiver partnership/employment status.
Excluded adolescents were slightly older and were more likely to come from households with lower incomes and lower caregiver educational attainment.
Effect sizes were generally small to modest.
No statistically significant differences were observed in sex or race/ethnicity (see Online Resource 1, Table S1).

text.text: For the transition analyses, transitions were defined using adjacent assessments (S02→S03, S03→S04, and S04→S05).

This approach ensured that observed changes in CU severity were localized to the period between consecutive assessments and that predictors were measured before the subsequent CU severity category was assessed.
Comparing nonadjacent assessments could obscure intermediate shifts in CU severity and make the timing of change less clear.

Across the 2,297 participants included in the trajectory analyses, 4,643 adjacent assessment intervals were available from 2,003 youth (87.2% of the trajectory sample); the remaining youth did not have CU data at two consecutive assessment waves and therefore could not contribute an adjacent assessment interval.
Of these 4,643 adjacent assessment intervals, 2,719 (58.6%) showed stability within the same CU severity category, whereas 1,924 (41.4%) showed movement between categories.
Because our aim was to examine shifts in CU severity, primary analyses included only assessment intervals during which adolescents moved between CU severity categories.

Thirty-six transition intervals (1.9%) were excluded because age or sex information from the core ABCD dataset was unavailable, resulting in a final analytic sample of 1,888 transition intervals contributed by 1,254 unique youth.
Because participants could contribute transitions across multiple pairs of adjacent assessments, the number of transition intervals exceeded the number of unique participants.

Callous-unemotional (CU) traits were assessed using the 15-item subset of the youthreport Inventory of Callous-Unemotional Traits (ICU) administered as part of the ABCD-SD Personality Disposition assessment.
Items were rated on a 4-point scale ranging from 0 (Does not apply at all) to 3 (Applies very well).
Seven positively worded items were reverse coded so that higher scores consistently reflected greater CU traits.
Item responses were summed to create a total score with a possible range of 0 to 45 for complete assessments.
Total scores were computed when at least 8 of the 15 items were completed.

Item-level missingness was minimal: 7,263 of 7,264 ICU assessments (99.99%) contained complete item responses, and the remaining assessment contained 14 of 15 responses and therefore met the prespecified scoring criterion.
No item-level imputation was performed.
Higher total scores indicated greater CU traits.

The full ICU has demonstrated acceptable reliability and construct validity across adolescent samples (Essau et al., 2006; Roose et al., 2010), with meta-analytic evidence supporting the reliability and external validity of the total score (Cardinale & Marsh, 2020).
text.formatted: The full ICU has demonstrated acceptable reliability and construct validity across adolescent samples <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Essau et al., 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Roose et al., 2010)</ref>, with meta-analytic evidence supporting the reliability and external validity of the total score <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Cardinale & Marsh, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Parenting practices were assessed using the youth-report Alabama Parenting Questionnaire (APQ).
In the ABCD-SD data, items were coded from 0 (Never) to 4 (Always).
Two composite scores were derived for the present analyses.
Positive parenting was calculated as the mean of 11 items assessing parental warmth, involvement, and positive parenting behaviors.
Negative parenting was calculated as the mean of 16 items assessing negative parenting practices, including poor monitoring and supervision, inconsistent discipline, and punitive parenting behaviors.
Higher mean scores reflected greater endorsement of the corresponding parenting dimension.
Composite scores were calculated when participants completed at least five items contributing to the relevant scale.
Among the 1,888 transition intervals included in the primary analyses, all positive-parenting assessments contained complete item responses.
Negative-parenting assessments were complete for 1,887 intervals, and the remaining interval contained 14 of 16 item responses and therefore met the prespecified scoring criterion.
No itemlevel imputation was performed.

The APQ has demonstrated acceptable reliability and validity in community samples of children and adolescents, with evidence supporting its factor structure and measurement across youth-and parent-report forms (Elgar et al., 2007; Florean et al., 2023; Russell et al., 2016).
text.formatted: The APQ has demonstrated acceptable reliability and validity in community samples of children and adolescents, with evidence supporting its factor structure and measurement across youth-and parent-report forms <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Elgar et al., 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Florean et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Russell et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Emotion dysregulation was assessed using the 36-item youth-report Difficulties in Emotion Regulation Scale (DERS).
In the ABCD-SD data, responses were coded from 0 to 4, with higher values indicating greater frequency.
Eleven positively worded items were reverse coded so that higher scores consistently reflected greater emotion dysregulation.
Item responses were averaged to create a total mean score.
Scores were computed when participants completed at least 10 of the 36 items.
All DERS assessments contained complete item responses, including those corresponding to the 1,888 transition intervals included in the primary analyses; no itemlevel imputation was performed.

Although the DERS assesses multiple facets of emotion regulation-including emotional identification, emotional clarity, impulse control, goal-directed behavior when distressed, and acceptance of emotional experiences-the present study examined only the overall emotion dysregulation score.
Higher scores reflected greater overall difficulties with emotion regulation.

The DERS has demonstrated good reliability and construct validity in adolescent community samples (Neumann et al., 2010), and its factor structure has been examined specifically among early adolescents in ABCD-SD (Smith et al., 2024).
text.formatted: The DERS has demonstrated good reliability and construct validity in adolescent community samples <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Neumann et al., 2010)</ref>, and its factor structure has been examined specifically among early adolescents in ABCD-SD <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Smith et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Delinquent behavior was included in sensitivity analyses to evaluate whether associations observed in the primary transition models remained after adjustment for prior or concurrent delinquency (see Sensitivity Analyses).
Delinquent behavior was assessed using the 48-item youth-report Self-Reported Delinquency Scale (SRD).
Items assessed engagement in a range of delinquent behaviors and were rated on a 3-point scale, with higher values indicating greater involvement in delinquent behavior.
Item responses were averaged to create a mean delinquency score.
Scores were computed when participants completed at least 20 of the 48 items.
Higher scores reflected greater overall involvement in delinquent behavior.
Fewer than 0.5% of SRD assessments failed to meet the prespecified scoring criterion.
Among the 1,888 transition intervals included in the primary analyses, valid baseline and wave-matched delinquency scores were available for all intervals; no item-level imputation was performed.

Self-report delinquency measures developed within the National Youth Survey have been extensively evaluated with respect to reliability and validity, including comparisons with official records of offending (Elliott et al., 1985; Huizinga & Elliott, 1986).
text.formatted: Self-report delinquency measures developed within the National Youth Survey have been extensively evaluated with respect to reliability and validity, including comparisons with official records of offending <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Elliott et al., 1985;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Huizinga & Elliott, 1986)</ref>.

text.text: For the sensitivity analyses, delinquent behavior was operationalized in two ways.

Baseline delinquency was derived from the lifetime delinquency assessment administered at ABCD-SD wave S01, whereas wave-matched delinquency was derived from the delinquency assessment collected at the beginning of each transition interval.
Age and sex were obtained from the core ABCD dataset and linked to ABCD-SD observations by participant identifier and corresponding assessment wave.
Because core ABCD and ABCD-SD assessments were not necessarily conducted concurrently, age from the corresponding core assessment served as an approximation of age at the ABCD-SD assessment.
Both variables were included as covariates in all primary transition and sensitivity regression models.
Age was treated as a continuous, mean-centered variable, and sex was coded as female or male.
Race/ethnicity, household income, highest caregiver education, and caregiver partnership/employment status were examined descriptively to characterize the analytic sample.
Latent class growth analysis (LCGA) was used to identify patterns of longitudinal CU development across adolescence.
Models were estimated in R using the flexmix package (Grün & Leisch, 2008), with model specification informed by the LCGA implementation described by Wardenaar (2022).
text.formatted: Models were estimated in R using the flexmix package <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Grün & Leisch, 2008)</ref>, with model specification informed by the LCGA implementation described by <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">Wardenaar (2022)</ref>.

text.text: Linear trajectories of CU traits were modeled as a function of assessment wave, with class-specific intercepts and linear slopes estimated while residual variance was constrained to equality across classes.

One-, two-, three-, and four-class solutions were estimated using all available CU assessments, allowing participants to contribute differing numbers of assessment waves and resulting in an unbalanced longitudinal design.
Models used 50 random starts and a maximum of 500 iterations to reduce local maxima.
The Akaike information criterion (AIC), Bayesian information criterion (BIC), and integrated completed likelihood (ICL) were used to compare competing models, with lower values indicating better fit.
Solutions containing classes representing fewer than 5% of the sample were considered less favorable for retention because of concerns regarding class size and interpretability.
The final model was selected based on the combined consideration of statistical fit, class size, parsimony, and substantive interpretability.
Participants were assigned to the trajectory corresponding to their highest posterior probability of class membership.

Differences in parenting and emotion dysregulation across the retained CU trajectory groups were examined using linear mixed-effects models with trajectory group and assessment wave as fixed effects and participant as a random intercept.
Tukey-adjusted pairwise comparisons of estimated marginal means, averaged across assessment waves, were used to compare trajectory groups.
Transition analyses examined within-person movement between relative levels of CU severity from one assessment to the next.

Observed Inventory of Callous-Unemotional Traits (ICU) scores at each assessment were categorized into low, moderate, and elevated CU severity using empirically derived cut points based on the pooled distribution of ICU scores across waves S02-S05.

Because validated clinical cutoffs are not available for the abbreviated ICU administered in the ABCD-SD Study, percentile-based cut points were used to define relative levels of CU severity while maintaining adequate observations within each category for stable estimation.
Scores ≤6 were classified as low severity, scores from 7 to 11 as moderate severity, and scores ≥12 as elevated severity.
These observed severity categories were conceptually distinct from the latent trajectory classes identified by the LCGA and were used solely to characterize movement between adjacent assessments.
Accordingly, transition categories were not derived from or conditioned on LCGA trajectory membership.
Transition observations were created by pairing adjacent assessments (S02→S03, S03→S04, and S04→S05).
Separate logistic regression models were estimated using assessment intervals in which adolescents changed CU severity categories, stratified by CU severity at the beginning of each interval.
Specifically, models compared transitions from low to elevated versus moderate severity, from moderate to elevated versus low severity, and from elevated to low versus moderate severity.
Positive parenting, negative parenting, and emotion dysregulation measured at the beginning of each interval were entered simultaneously as predictors of subsequent CU severity.
All models were adjusted for age and sex, as described above.

Because some transition types became infrequent when analyses were further stratified by assessment interval, particularly among adolescents beginning at elevated CU severity, transition intervals were pooled across adjacent assessment intervals for the primary analyses.
Pooling increased statistical stability while allowing estimation of overall associations between beginning-of-interval predictors and subsequent CU severity across adolescence.
Cluster-robust standard errors were used to account for multiple transition intervals contributed by the same participant.
Positive parenting, negative parenting, and emotion dysregulation were standardized using the pooled transition sample before estimating the primary and interval-specific models.
Delinquency variables were standardized for sensitivity analyses, and age was mean-centered.

Accordingly, odds ratios for standardized continuous predictors represent the multiplicative change in the odds of the modeled transition associated with a one-standard-deviation increase in the predictor, holding other variables constant.
Odds ratios for age represent the corresponding change associated with a one-year increase, whereas odds ratios for sex represent the comparison between the coded categories.
Interval-specific models were subsequently estimated as sensitivity analyses to evaluate whether associations were consistent across assessment intervals (see Online Resource 1, Tables S4-S5).

text.text: Interval-specific sensitivity analyses evaluated whether associations from the primary transition models were consistent across assessment periods by re-estimating the logistic regression models separately within each interval.

Because statistical evidence for an association between emotion dysregulation and transition outcomes was weaker during the final assessment interval, supplementary resampling analyses evaluated the extent to which interval-specific differences in sample size may have contributed to this pattern (see Online Resource 1, Table S6).

text.text: Stability and Movement Across Assessment Waves Among 2,003 youth who completed at least one pair of consecutive CU assessments, 730 (36.4%) remained within the same CU severity category across all observed intervals, whereas 738 (36.8%) experienced one transition between severity categories.
The remaining 535 youth (26.7%) experienced multiple transitions, including 419 (20.9%) who transitioned twice and 116 (5.8%) who transitioned during all three observed intervals.
Overall, 63.6% of youth experienced at least one transition between CU severity categories.
Among the 630 transitions beginning at low CU severity, 465 (73.8%) were to moderate severity and 165 (26.2%) were to elevated severity.
Of the 837 transitions beginning at moderate severity, 378 (45.2%) were to low severity and 459 (54.8%) were to elevated severity.
Similarly, among the 421 transitions beginning at elevated severity, 86 (20.4%) were to low severity and 335 (79.6%) were to moderate severity.
Overall, transitions between adjacent severity categories were more common than direct movement between low and elevated severity (Figure 2; see Online Resource 1, Table S3).

text.text: The present study examined patterns of callous-unemotional (CU) trait development across adolescence by integrating person-centered trajectory analyses with wave-to-wave transitions between observed CU severity categories.

Latent class growth analyses identified three distinct developmental trajectories characterized by low, moderate, and elevated CU traits that remained differentiated across adolescence, with differences between groups primarily reflecting overall CU levels rather than rates of change.
However, substantial movement between CU severity categories occurred across successive assessments.

Among adolescents who transitioned, greater positive parenting was associated with movement toward lower severity among moderate-start adolescents and with smaller increases among low-start adolescents.
Greater negative parenting was associated with movement toward higher severity among moderate-start adolescents.
Greater emotion dysregulation was associated with movement toward higher severity among moderate-start adolescents and with larger increases among lowstart adolescents.

Together, these findings show that relatively stable developmental trajectories can occur alongside substantial changes in CU severity across adolescence, and that the factors associated with changes in CU severity depend on adolescents' starting level of CU severity.

All three trajectory groups demonstrated modest increases in CU traits across adolescence, with differences between groups primarily reflecting their overall levels of CU traits rather than pronounced differences in rates of change.

This pattern resembles findings from justice-involved males, among whom relatively stable low, moderate, and high CU trajectories were identified across adolescence and early adulthood (Baskin-Sommers et al., 2015).
text.formatted: This pattern resembles findings from justice-involved males, among whom relatively stable low, moderate, and high CU trajectories were identified across adolescence and early adulthood <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Baskin-Sommers et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: In contrast, studies beginning earlier in development have identified stable-high, increasing, decreasing, and low trajectories (Fanti et al., 2017).
text.formatted: In contrast, studies beginning earlier in development have identified stable-high, increasing, decreasing, and low trajectories <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Fanti et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Other work has identified increasing joint profiles of CU traits and conduct disorder symptoms, suggesting that observed developmental patterns may also depend on whether CU traits are examined independently or alongside other externalizing behaviors (Eisenbarth et al., 2016).

text.text: Collectively, these findings suggest that the number and shape of CU trajectories may vary according to developmental period, sample characteristics, measurement approach, and analytic strategy.

Thus, the absence of pronounced increasing or decreasing trajectories in the present study should be interpreted as characterizing patterns of CU development in this community sample, rather than evidence that such trajectories do not occur.
The parenting findings support a distinction between positive and negative dimensions of the caregiving environment in CU development.

Greater positive parenting predicted movement toward lower severity among moderate-start adolescents and movement to moderate rather than elevated severity among low-start adolescents, whereas greater negative parenting predicted movement toward higher severity among moderate-start adolescents.

Although these associations emerged across different starting levels, their direction was consistent with longitudinal evidence linking warm, positive parenting to lower subsequent CU traits and harsh or unsupportive parenting to higher CU traits (Waller et al., 2013 (Waller et al., , 2014;; Waller, Baskin-Sommers, & Hyde, 2018).

text.text: However, the association with negative parenting was attenuated after adjustment for delinquency, whereas associations with positive parenting were more robust to this adjustment.

This attenuation may reflect overlapping associations of negative parenting with both CU traits and broader externalizing behaviors, consistent with prior evidence linking negative parenting to elevated externalizing symptoms (Brady et al., 2024).

text.text: Together, these findings suggest that parenting is relevant to CU development during adolescence, with particularly consistent evidence for positive parenting.

Parenting may be particularly relevant to CU development because the capacities that CU traits disrupt, including empathy, guilt, and concern for others, develop in part through repeated interactions with caregivers.

Developmental models propose that warm, responsive parenting supports the emergence of empathy and prosocial behavior, whereas low warmth and harsh parenting heighten risk for CU behavior, particularly among youth with existing vulnerabilities (Waller & Hyde, 2018).
text.formatted: Developmental models propose that warm, responsive parenting supports the emergence of empathy and prosocial behavior, whereas low warmth and harsh parenting heighten risk for CU behavior, particularly among youth with existing vulnerabilities <ref type="bibr">(Waller & Hyde, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Consistent with this account, parental warmth and positive expressiveness have been linked longitudinally with empathy-related responding and social functioning (Zhou et al., 2002).
text.formatted: Consistent with this account, parental warmth and positive expressiveness have been linked longitudinally with empathy-related responding and social functioning <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">(Zhou et al., 2002)</ref>.

text.text: The present findings extend this work in two ways.

First, they suggest that these caregiving processes remain relevant in adolescence, a period when peer influences grow and parental influence is often assumed to wane (Brown & Bakken, 2011; Meyer et al., 2026).
text.formatted: First, they suggest that these caregiving processes remain relevant in adolescence, a period when peer influences grow and parental influence is often assumed to wane <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Brown & Bakken, 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Meyer et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Second, they show that parenting is associated not only with stable differences in CU traits between adolescents, but also with the direction of change among adolescents who shift between CU severity levels.
The distinction between positive and negative parenting also appears in intervention research, which further suggests that parenting is a potentially modifiable target.

In the Fast Track trial, intervention-related increases in parental warmth were indirectly associated with lower subsequent CU traits, whereas reductions in harsh discipline were associated with lower conduct disorder symptoms (Pasalich et al., 2016).
text.formatted: In the Fast Track trial, intervention-related increases in parental warmth were indirectly associated with lower subsequent CU traits, whereas reductions in harsh discipline were associated with lower conduct disorder symptoms <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Pasalich et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Parent training has also produced reductions in CU traits among children with conduct problems (Fleming et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Parent training has also produced reductions in CU traits among children with conduct problems <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Fleming et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Together with the present findings, this work suggests that positive and negative parenting may relate to CU traits through distinct processes, and that interventions targeting CU traits may benefit from building warmth in addition to reducing harshness.

The present findings suggest that parenting remains relevant to changes in CU severity during adolescence and highlight the importance of testing whether strengthening positive parenting and reducing negative parenting can alter CU development during this period.

Greater emotion dysregulation predicted movement toward higher CU severity among moderate-start adolescents and movement directly from low to elevated severity, rather than from low to moderate severity, among low-start adolescents.
These findings suggest that emotion dysregulation may be relevant to changes in CU severity even among adolescents who do not initially show elevated CU traits.

More broadly, difficulties in regulating emotion have been implicated in adolescent externalizing behavior and may contribute to persistent patterns of maladaptive responding (Baskin-Sommers et al., 2022; Modecki et al., 2017).
text.formatted: More broadly, difficulties in regulating emotion have been implicated in adolescent externalizing behavior and may contribute to persistent patterns of maladaptive responding <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Baskin-Sommers et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Modecki et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: One possibility is that adolescents who have difficulty regulating negative emotions, such as anger or frustration, may be more likely to respond impulsively or aggressively during interpersonal conflict.
Difficulties tolerating distress may also reinforce these responses when they provide temporary relief from negative emotions (Baskin-Sommers et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Difficulties tolerating distress may also reinforce these responses when they provide temporary relief from negative emotions <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Baskin-Sommers et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Over time, repeated difficulties managing distress and inhibiting maladaptive responses could contribute to increasing CU severity, although specific processes underlying this association require further investigation.
Thus, emotion dysregulation may reflect a vulnerability that increases risk for rising CU severity in some adolescents, rather than a defining feature of CU traits themselves.
The present findings suggest that emotion regulation may be an important consideration address processes specific to CU traits (Perlstein et al., 2023; Waaler et al., 2024).

text.text: The meaning of each transition depended on adolescents' starting CU severity.

The moderate-start analysis provided the clearest test of direction because both possible destinations were adjacent to the starting category and represented movement toward lower or higher CU severity in absolute terms.
Among these adolescents, greater positive parenting predicted movement toward low severity, whereas greater negative parenting and emotion dysregulation predicted movement toward elevated severity.
These findings indicate that parenting and emotion dysregulation distinguish the direction of change among adolescents starting from the same level of CU severity.
The low-and elevated-start analyses address a different question.
Adolescents starting at low severity could only move upward, so the contrast distinguished a smaller shift to moderate severity from a larger shift directly to elevated severity.
Likewise, adolescents starting at elevated severity could only move downward, so the contrast distinguished a shift to moderate severity from a larger shift directly to low severity.
These models therefore inform the magnitude of change within a single direction rather than the direction itself.

Among low-start adolescents, greater positive parenting was associated with moving to moderate rather than elevated severity, suggesting that positive parenting may be associated with smaller increases when CU severity rises.
In contrast, greater emotion dysregulation was associated with moving to elevated rather than moderate severity, suggesting that dysregulation may be associated with larger increases.
Because relatively few adolescents moved directly from low to elevated severity, findings from the low-start model should be interpreted with caution and replicated in larger samples.
Distinguishing these contrasts has implications for both research and prevention.
Methodologically, trajectory analyses alone would have obscured these findings, as they summarize each adolescent's overall pattern rather than the shifts that occur between assessments.
Examining transitions conditional on starting severity revealed that the same factors may relate to different aspects of change depending on where adolescents begin.

For adolescents with moderate levels of CU traits, parenting and emotion dysregulation were associated with whether severity subsequently decreased or increased, suggesting that this group may be at a developmental crossroads where caregiving and regulatory factors are linked to the direction of change.

For adolescents with low CU traits who showed increases, positive parenting and emotion dysregulation were associated with how large those increases were, suggesting that these factors may help identify youth at risk for larger increases in CU severity.

If replicated in designs capable of testing causal effects, these patterns could inform prevention efforts tailored to adolescents' current CU severity, such as strengthening caregiving among youth with moderate traits or targeting emotion regulation among low-severity youth who show signs of rising CU traits.
Before concluding, several limitations should be acknowledged.

First, although the longitudinal design established temporal ordering between predictors measured at the beginning of an assessment interval and subsequent CU severity, the observational nature of the study precludes causal inference.
Parenting, emotion dysregulation, and CU traits may influence one another reciprocally over development.
For example, in younger children, greater parental warmth predicts lower subsequent CU behavior, while higher CU behavior also predicts lower subsequent parental warmth (Waller et al., 2014).
text.formatted: For example, in younger children, greater parental warmth predicts lower subsequent CU behavior, while higher CU behavior also predicts lower subsequent parental warmth <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Waller et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Such reciprocal processes may be especially relevant during adolescence, as youth increasingly shape their interactions with caregivers.

Thus, although parenting was measured before each transition, the present analyses cannot determine whether parenting contributes to changes in CU severity, reflects caregivers' responses to existing characteristics, or both.
Unmeasured individual, family, or contextual factors may contribute to the observed associations.
Accordingly, the present findings identify prospective correlates of changes in CU severity rather than causal mechanisms.

Future research using designs that explicitly model reciprocal processes, as well as intervention studies that directly manipulate parenting or emotion regulation processes, will be important for determining whether these prospective associations reflect modifiable mechanisms of CU development.
Second, the study relied primarily on youth self-report measures of CU traits, parenting, emotion dysregulation, and delinquent behavior.

Although youth reports provide important information about adolescents' internal experiences and perceptions of their family environments, reliance on a common informant may increase shared-method variance and may not fully capture these constructs from other perspectives.

Future research incorporating parent and teacher reports, observational measures of parent-child interactions, behavioral assessments, and clinical evaluations could determine whether the present findings generalize across informants and methods.
Third, attrition across assessment waves resulted in fewer observations at later assessments and reduced precision for analyses conducted at later intervals.
This limitation was particularly relevant when models were stratified by both starting CU severity and assessment interval, resulting in relatively small numbers for some transition types.
Participants also contributed differing numbers of adjacent assessment intervals, resulting in unequal opportunities to exhibit a transition across the study period.

The supplementary resampling analyses suggested that reduced sample size may have contributed to weaker statistical evidence for emotion dysregulation at the final interval, underscoring the need for caution when interpreting differences across assessment periods.
Longer-term studies with greater retention could clarify whether these associations persist across adolescence.
Finally, the present study was conducted in a community sample, which may limit generalizability to populations characterized by higher levels of CU traits, behavioral problems, or contextual risk.

Replication in clinical and justice-involved samples will therefore be important for determining whether the observed associations between parenting, emotion dysregulation, and changes in CU severity extend to youth with more persistent externalizing problems.
The present study extends research on CU development by examining both developmental trajectories and shifts between CU severity levels across adolescence.
Although low, moderate, and elevated trajectories remained differentiated over time, many adolescents moved between severity levels from one assessment to the next.
Among those who changed, positive parenting was associated with lower subsequent CU severity, whereas negative parenting and emotion dysregulation were associated with higher subsequent severity.

Examining transitions alongside trajectories therefore provides a more complete picture of CU development, distinguishing not only whether adolescents move toward lower or higher severity, but also, for those starting at low severity, how large those shifts are.

Broadly, these findings suggest that CU traits in adolescence are less fixed than stable group trajectories imply, and that modifiable features of youths' family and emotional lives are associated with how CU severity changes across adolescence and the direction their development takes.

Tukey-adjusted pairwise comparisons of estimated marginal means, averaged across assessment waves, were conducted to evaluate differences between trajectory groups.

To evaluate whether associations between parenting, emotion dysregulation, and changes in CU severity were consistent across assessment intervals, the primary transition models were re-estimated separately for each adjacent assessment interval (S02→S03, S03→S04, and S04→S05).
Analyses included only intervals in which adolescents transitioned between CU severity categories.
Models were stratified by starting CU severity and included positive parenting, negative parenting, and emotion dysregulation simultaneously, with adjustment for age and sex.

Because statistical evidence for the association between emotion dysregulation and changes in CU severity was weaker during the final assessment interval, an additional resampling analysis evaluated the extent to which reduced sample size may have contributed to this pattern.
